newsitem.title: FRANCE: French book says Drummond murder was Cold War plot.
newsitem.headline: French book says Drummond murder was Cold War plot.

text.p: British scientist Sir Jack Drummond, murdered with his family in southern France in 1952, fell victim to a Soviet Cold War plot rather than to the French farmer who was convicted, a newly published book says.
The murder of Drummond, his wife Anne and their 10-year-old daughter Elizabeth on a remote river bank near the southern village of Lurs was post-World War Two France's most famous crime riddle.

The fatal encounter of a scientist involved in wartime secrets and the closely knit Dominici clan of backwards French peasants in the romantic hills of upper Provence, fascinated the country and stuck in French memory as "the Dominici case".
"The 'Dominici case' was ill-named. Actually it is the 'Drummond case'," French journalist William Reymond said in his book "Dominici Not Guilty - The Murderers Uncovered".

He called for a new probe, saying he had found evidence that the Drummonds were killed by a hit squad on Soviet orders because of his alleged secret service activity and that an embarrassed French government covered up the plot.
Drummond and his wife, on a French holiday, were shot and their daughter was bludgeoned to death with a rifle butt as they camped at night near the Dominici's sheep and olive farm.
After a year-long investigation often criticised as bungled, the clan's 76-year-old illiterate patriarch, Gaston Dominici was accused of the murder by his sons Gustave and Clovis.
He confessed to the killings, saying Drummond caught him as he watched his wife undress. Despite retracting his confession, he was sentenced to death by guillotine in 1954.
The sentence was commuted to life in prison because of his age. He was pardoned by President Charles de Gaulle in 1960 and died five years later.
Dominici's grandson Alain is campaigning to rehabilitate him, and his lawyer Gilbert Collard formally requested a re-trial last week to take account of Reymond's findings.

Drummond, 61, a famed nutritionist, was knighted during World War Two for inventing liquid food substitutes said to have helped millions through food shortages, including a so-called blitzbroth fed to Londoners in bomb shelters.
British newspapers have reported that he was a member of the Intelligence Service during the war and worked on the secret Porton Down chemical weapons project.
Citing U.S. evidence, Reymond alleged that Drummond remained a secret agent and was involved in post-war Anglo-American bids to recruit Nazi scientists and counter similar Soviet attempts.
"In 1952, at least three scientists fell victims to the Soviet response: German Erich Kramer, and two Britons, Dr Peck...and Sir Jack Drummond," he wrote.

Reymond alleged he obtained German Landespolizei records of the police questioning of a petty criminal, William Bartkowski, detained in the German city of Stuttgart four days after the murders in Lurs, 80 km (50 miles) northeast of Marseille.

He wrote that Bartkowski had said he was recruited by the Soviets to kill Kramer and he described in troubling detail how his four-man squad killed the Drummonds. He named his accomplices as a Greek called Carlo Solet, a Swiss named only as Moradis and a Spaniard called Roman Moesto.

French police were told of the confession at the time, but dismissed Bartkowski as a liar who had read about the Lurs murders in the press and was playing for time in order to obtain a prison transfer and plan an escape.

Reymond accused French police of ignoring Bartkowski on Interior Ministry orders. "A state could not admit that a squad armed by the Soviets had been able to hit foreign nationals, in the heart of France, under the nose of its counter-espionnage, military and police," he wrote.
Veteran reporter Jean Laborde, who covered the investigation and Dominici trial for the daily France-Soir, dismissed the book as "ressuscitated old stories" long denied by Britain.
"What could have been Britain's interest in concealing the truth and a motive that could have explained the murders?" he asked.
